narrative_idea_gen: Two rival homicide detectives—Manny Salazar and Doug Phelan—who've been reluctantly desk-neighbors for fourteen years and share an unshakable bond built entirely on arguing about break room etiquette, thermostat settings, and whose turn it is to replace the Brita filter, must each independently assemble competing task forces of retired cops, jittery forensic accountants, and one inexplicably loyal hotdog vendor to crack a counterfeiting ring operating from a gutted mattress warehouse in Queens. The entire story is narrated by Cheryl Kang-Moretti, their desk sergeant, whose omniscient insight into both men's inner lives comes from fifteen years of reading their incident reports, intercepting their passive-aggressive Post-it wars, and monitoring their group chats—and she structures her account through those very artifacts: evidence logs, insurance claim forms, Yelp reviews of the precinct, and margin doodles that grow increasingly heartbroken as she realizes the case is quietly destroying the one good thing either man has. Everything collides when both teams breach the warehouse simultaneously alongside the actual criminals, and every gun lowers in stunned unison as Manny and Doug—oblivious to their audience of forty—erupt into a raw, shaking argument about why Doug hid his terminal diagnosis for nine months, turning a tactical disaster into a moment of collective human paralysis that even the counterfeiters can't bring themselves to interrupt. Cheryl files the final report knowing the partnership is over not because they failed, but because Doug succeeded in pushing Manny far enough away that grief might not break him—an act of love she can only document, never fix, in twelve-point Times New Roman.

narrative_beats:
# Seven Structural Beats for *The Brita Filter Incident* (Working Title)

---

## Beat 1: The Bureaucratic Frame Opens — and Immediately Confesses Its Own Bias

**What to Write:** Cheryl Kang-Moretti introduces herself not as a narrator but as a *filing instrument*. She presents the first artifact — perhaps a standard NYPD incident summary or an insurance claim form for water damage in the break room — annotated with her own marginal notes. Through this document, we learn that two homicide detectives, Manny Salazar and Doug Phelan, have been desk-neighbors for fourteen years. The opening artifact should appear to be about something trivially bureaucratic (a thermostat complaint, a missing Brita filter) but should contain, buried in the boilerplate language, the first hint that something has recently ended.

**Narrative Technique — The False Bureaucracy:** Just as Borges opens with a footnote-style correction of a real historian and a deposition with missing pages, Cheryl's narration must establish from the first paragraph that we are reading *institutional paperwork that has been colonized by a human voice*. The form is the frame. An evidence log header, an interdepartmental memo, a Yelp review of the 108th Precinct ("two stars — the sergeant at the desk seemed distracted and sad") — these are the fragments from which the reader reconstructs reality. The key move: Cheryl must acknowledge early that her "omniscience" is constructed. She knows these men because she has read fourteen years of their paperwork, intercepted their Post-it wars, monitored their group chats. Her narration is forensic, not mystical. This makes her authority simultaneously total and heartbreakingly limited — she has all the evidence and none of the power to intervene.

**Why This Beat Matters:** The reader must be disoriented about genre in exactly the way Borges disorients — *are we reading a police procedural? A comedy about office life? A case file?* The answer is yes to all, and the ambiguity is the point. But more critically, the opening document must do what Borges's missing pages do: perform the story's theme before the reader knows what the theme is. Cheryl is a person who can only love through documentation. The entire story is an act of love disguised as a filing obligation. If the first beat doesn't establish that the *form itself is the emotional argument*, everything downstream collapses into mere cleverness. Start with a small artifact. Let it be funny. Let something in its margins be quietly wrong.

---

## Beat 2: The Counterfeiting Case Arrives and Both Men Seize It — for Reasons Neither Will Name

**What to Write:** A counterfeiting ring is identified operating from a gutted mattress warehouse in Queens. The case lands on or near Manny's and Doug's desks — perhaps through a jurisdictional accident, perhaps because a body tangentially connected to their homicide caseload surfaces with counterfeit bills in its pockets. What matters: both men independently decide to build competing task forces to crack the case. This is presented through parallel artifacts — Manny's task force roster filed at 2:47 PM, Doug's filed at 3:12 PM the same day, neither referencing the other. Cheryl annotates the coincidence. She notes that Doug's handwriting has changed in recent months — smaller, more careful, as though conserving energy. She does not yet tell us why she notices this.

**Narrative Technique — The Clock of Rivalry as Love's Disguise:** Borrow Borges's "clock of pursuit" compression. Where Yu Tsun lays out his monstrous plan with chess-player detachment, Manny and Doug each assemble their task forces with the same cold, competitive logic — except the reader should sense, through Cheryl's documentary apparatus, that the competition is not rational. These men have fourteen years of shared cases. They could collaborate. That they don't — that they *choose* to fork — is the first structural mystery. Doug's decision to build a rival team should feel, on first read, like petty one-upmanship. On reread, it should be legible as the first move in his real plan: to make Manny angry enough to let go. The task force rosters themselves should be comic and lovingly specific. Retired cops lured back with vague promises. Jittery forensic accountants who speak only in spreadsheet metaphors. And one inexplicably loyal hot dog vendor, whose presence on Doug's team Cheryl documents with a mixture of bafflement and grudging admiration.

**Why This Beat Matters:** This is where the dual engine ignites. The counterfeiting case is the *spy plot* — the genre machinery that propels the narrative forward. The rivalry is the *metaphysical plot* — the deeper story about two men whose bond is built entirely on friction, and what happens when one of them decides to use that friction as a weapon of mercy. Establish both engines here. Make the case feel real and procedurally grounded (Cheryl would insist on this). Make the rivalry feel absurd and petty (the Post-it war should escalate — accusations about the Brita filter, thermostat sabotage, a passive-aggressive group chat message about "professional boundaries"). But plant, through Cheryl's marginal annotations, the tiny evidentiary anomalies that will later reveal the second story hiding inside the first: Doug is dying, and every provocation is a goodbye.

---

## Beat 3: The Parallel Investigations Unfold — Two Forking Paths Through the Same Precinct

**What to Write:** Present the two investigations in interleaved documentary fragments. Manny's team works one angle (following the paper trail — the forensic accountants shine here). Doug's team works another (street-level, old-school, the hot dog vendor turns out to have a cart stationed near the warehouse and has been inadvertently surveilling it for months). The fragments should include: evidence logs with conflicting chain-of-custody signatures, dueling whiteboard photographs (Cheryl photographs both), intercepted group chat messages in which each man complains about the other to his own team, and at least one Yelp review of a Queens establishment visited during the investigation that contains, in its mundane consumer language, an accidental piece of critical intelligence.

**Narrative Technique — The Literal Made Figural (and Vice Versa):** This beat mirrors Borges's walk down the forking lane — the instruction to "always turn left" that is simultaneously practical and thematic. Here, the *forking* is the two parallel investigations. The structural conceit must be felt physically by the reader: the artifacts *alternate*, the documentary fragments from Manny's team and Doug's team interleave, and the reader is literally walking two paths through the same narrative landscape. But the forking is also figural. Every petty argument about the Brita filter or the thermostat is also, in retrospect, an argument about something else entirely: *How do you take care of someone? What does it cost to be the one who always replaces the filter? What does it mean that Doug has stopped fighting about the thermostat?*

Cheryl's margin doodles should begin appearing in this section. Small drawings in the edges of photocopied forms. At first humorous — caricatures of Manny's exasperated face, Doug's theatrical shrug. Then, as the beat progresses, the doodles shift. A coffee cup drawn with too much care. A chair drawn empty. Cheryl is tracking something she hasn't consciously articulated, and her hand knows before her prose does.

**Why This Beat Matters:** Suspense through beauty — Borges delays the murder by making the walk to Albert's house gorgeous and dreamlike. Here, delay the collision by making the parallel investigations *funny, warm, and procedurally absorbing*. Let the reader enjoy the comedy of two rival task forces tripping over each other in the same borough. Let the hot dog vendor be genuinely, surprisingly good at surveillance. Let the forensic accountants have a panic attack that accidentally reveals a key connection. The reader should be having a wonderful time. That pleasure is what makes Beat 6 devastating. The comedy is the raised blade. The reader must not see it as such. Build the case. Build the rivalry. Build the love — but call it irritation, call it habit, call it the argument about whose turn it is to buy coffee. The audience should be laughing when the doodles start to go sad. They should notice only on the second or third sad doodle that something has changed.

---

## Beat 4: Cheryl Discovers the Diagnosis — Through Paperwork, Because That Is How She Knows Everything

**Concrete Action:** Cheryl encounters an artifact that does not belong in the case file. Perhaps a misfiled insurance form. Perhaps a request for leave that was drafted but never submitted. Perhaps a prescription receipt that fell out of a folder. Whatever it is, it tells her — in the clinical, bureaucratic language she has spent fifteen years reading — that Doug Phelan has a terminal diagnosis and has known for approximately nine months. She now re-reads every artifact from the preceding months. She presents some of them again for the reader, and they are transformed.

**Narrative Technique — Dramatic Irony as Vertigo, Inverted:** In Borges, the reader knows Yu Tsun has come to kill Albert while Albert warmly welcomes him. Here, invert the structure: Cheryl (and the reader) discover the terminal diagnosis while *looking backward* at hospitality already extended. Every kind provocation Doug aimed at Manny — every stolen Post-it, every thermostat sabotage, every refusal to collaborate on the case — is retroactively revealed as an act of deliberate, architectural cruelty-as-love. Doug has been constructing a version of himself that Manny will be *relieved* to lose. The dramatic irony lands not as suspense about the future but as horror about the past. We re-enter scenes we've already read and find them full of ghosts.

Cheryl's reaction must be rendered through her documentary voice — controlled, precise, formatted. But the control should crack. A sentence that starts in proper report syntax and derails. A margin note that is just a date, circled, circled again. The restraint *is* the grief. She cannot call Doug. She cannot tell Manny. She is a desk sergeant. She files things.

**Why This Beat Matters:** This is the structural hinge of the entire story — the moment when the reader's understanding of every prior beat bifurcates. What was comedy becomes elegy. What was rivalry becomes a terminal patient's strategic withdrawal from the person who would grieve him most. The "competing task forces" are not competing — they are Doug's mechanism for building distance. The Brita filter arguments are not petty — they are Doug maintaining the texture of normalcy while he dismantles the partnership from within. This beat must land with the force of Borges's revelation that the labyrinth and the novel are the same object. The thing you thought was one kind of story is another kind of story, and it always was, and you were reading both at the same time.

---

## Beat 5: Cheryl Re-Narrates the Partnership — The Artifacts Read Back as Elegy

**What to Write:** Cheryl now presents the definitive history of the Salazar-Phelan partnership, drawn from fifteen years of incident reports, Post-it notes, margin doodles, and group chat logs. This is the "expository revelation as climax" — a section that pauses the forward momentum of the case to deliver the story's emotional and thematic core. She traces the partnership through its accumulation of trivial rituals: who sits where, who makes the coffee run, the unspoken rules of the Post-it war, the specific brand of filter Doug always bought, the thermostat number (68°F, always 68°F, and the war is about the fact that the thermostat *sticks* and someone has to *jiggle it* and neither will admit to being the jiggler). Through these artifacts, Cheryl constructs a theory of love that operates entirely through friction — a bond that exists only because both parties refuse to admit it exists, expressed exclusively through complaint.

**Narrative Technique — The Expository Heart as Structural Climax:** Borges makes Albert's lecture on the forking-paths novel the dramatic peak of a spy thriller. Here, make Cheryl's documentary reconstruction of a fourteen-year desk-neighbor relationship the emotional peak of a crime story. The counterfeiting case should be *suspended* during this beat — we are mid-investigation, the warehouse breach is coming, but Cheryl *stops the procedural machinery* to file what amounts to a love letter in the form of an institutional retrospective. This is where the margin doodles reach their most heartbroken — a series of small drawings that Cheryl herself identifies as a record she didn't know she was keeping.

The key structural move: embed within this retrospective the equivalent of Ts'ui Pên's riddle. Somewhere in the archive of artifacts, there is a pattern that Cheryl identifies — a change in Doug's behavior that began exactly nine months ago. A Post-it war that suddenly escalated. A Brita filter that stopped getting replaced. The thermostat left at the wrong temperature without complaint. Doug was *erasing his own habits* so that the space he would leave behind would already feel empty. He was pre-grieving himself out of the room.

**Why This Beat Matters:** This beat is the story's equivalent of Beat 5 in Borges — the moment when the philosophical frame achieves its fullest expression inside the dramatic situation. The "forking paths" here are the two ways to read every artifact: as comedy or as elegy. The reader now holds both simultaneously, just as Borges's reader holds espionage and metaphysics in the same sentence. Cheryl's narration must make the reader *feel* the forking — the version of this story where Doug's pettiness is just pettiness and the version where it is the most sophisticated act of preemptive grief management ever committed through office supplies. Both versions are true. The story's power comes from their superposition.

---

## Beat 6: The Warehouse Breach — Every Gun Lowers

**What to Write:** Both task forces converge on the mattress warehouse simultaneously. Manny's team enters from one side. Doug's team enters from the other. The actual counterfeiters are present, mid-operation. For a brief, slapstick moment, the scene is pure tactical disaster — forty people in a room, guns drawn, no one certain who is on whose side, the hot dog vendor inexplicably holding a condiment gun that is briefly mistaken for a weapon. Then Manny and Doug see each other across the warehouse floor. And
narrative_story:
# The Brita Filter Incident

## A Documentary Reconstruction by Cheryl Kang-Moretti, Desk Sergeant, 108th Precinct, Long Island City, Queens

Filed pursuant to no particular regulation. Cross-referenced with nothing anyone asked for.

---

## I.

**ARTIFACT 1-A: INTERDEPARTMENTAL FACILITIES REQUEST FORM (FORM 77-B), DATED MARCH 4**

**SUBMITTED BY:** Det. Emmanuel "Manny" Salazar, Shield #4412
**NATURE OF REQUEST:** Replacement of one (1) Brita Longlast+ water filtration pitcher, white, 10-cup capacity, currently stationed on shared counter adjacent to Desks 7 and 8, Second Floor, Homicide/Major Crimes
**REASON FOR REQUEST:** Current unit is "functionally deceased" due to failure of neighboring detective to replace filter cartridge at any point in the preceding calendar quarter despite posted schedule (see attached Post-it, Exhibit A) and despite the fact that water now tastes, quote, "like someone dissolved a MetroCard in it"
**COST CENTER:** Det. Salazar requests the expense be charged to Det. D. Phelan's overtime budget "since he apparently has time to do everything except basic maintenance of shared resources"
**STATUS:** Denied (no such cost-center transfer exists)

---

*Cheryl's note, appended in blue pen along left margin:*

I am filing this because it is my function to file things. I want that on the record before anyone accuses this document of being something it isn't. I have been the desk sergeant of the 108th Precinct for fifteen years. In that time I have processed upward of forty thousand interdepartmental forms, eleven thousand incident reports, six hundred and twelve complaints about the second-floor men's room, and one (1) heartfelt letter of resignation that turned out to be a draft of someone's wedding vows run through the wrong printer tray. I processed that too. It is not my job to editorialize. It is my job to receive, stamp, date, route, and archive.

If I have, in the process of receiving, stamping, dating, routing, and archiving, also developed certain *observations* about the people who generate the paperwork I process — well. Paper is transparent if you hold it up to the light long enough. You learn things. You learn that Detective Salazar writes in all caps when he's angry and in a cramped lowercase cursive when he's thinking. You learn that Detective Phelan has never once submitted a form on time but has never once submitted one with a factual error. You learn that two men who have sat at adjacent desks for fourteen years and seven months generate a particular *frequency* of paperwork — facilities requests, overtime disputes, thermostat complaints, passive-aggressive Post-it notes photographed and submitted as "evidence of hostile work environment" with a winking parenthetical indicating the submission is "mostly a joke" — and that this frequency is, or was, a kind of language.

I am not the narrator of this story. I am its filing system. The distinction matters.

But a filing system is allowed to notice when the frequency changes.

---

**ARTIFACT 1-B: YELP REVIEW, "108TH PRECINCT — LONG ISLAND CITY," POSTED FEBRUARY 27 BY USER "queens4lyfe_karen"**

★★☆☆☆

Went to file a noise complaint about my neighbor's emotional support parrot. The sergeant at the front desk (older woman, Korean maybe, very organized) seemed distracted and sad about something. She stamped my form three times. I said "Is everything okay?" and she said "Fine, the third stamp is for our records" but I don't think that was true because one of the stamps was upside down. Also there was yelling from upstairs, which I assume is normal for a police station but it sounded personal. Two stars because they did take the complaint. The parrot situation is ongoing.

---

*Cheryl's note, appended on a separate sheet and stapled to the printed review:*

The stamp was not upside down. I use a secondary orientation to flag forms requiring follow-up. This is my system. It has been my system since 2011. I don't expect a civilian to understand institutional notation, and I don't expect Yelp to be a reliable source of emotional intelligence.

I was not sad. I was processing an anomaly.

The yelling was Detectives Salazar and Phelan. It was about the thermostat, nominally. The thermostat on the second floor has a sticking mechanism that requires manual adjustment — a specific lateral pressure followed by a clockwise quarter-turn — and for fourteen years neither detective has admitted to being the one who performs this adjustment, though the thermostat is always at 68°F by 9:15 AM, which means someone does it, and the someone arrives before 9:15 AM, which narrows the candidates to two. On February 27, the thermostat read 64°F at 11:00 AM and no one had touched it.

That was the anomaly.

I should not have noticed. But I process the heating-system work orders. I know the rhythm. And the rhythm had stumbled.

---

**ARTIFACT 1-C: INCIDENT SUMMARY FORM (ISF-3), DATED MARCH 7 — WATER DAMAGE, SECOND FLOOR BREAK ROOM**

**REPORTING OFFICER:** Sgt. C. Kang-Moretti
**INCIDENT:** At approximately 14:20 hours, the Brita Longlast+ water filtration pitcher stationed in the second-floor break room was found shattered on the linoleum floor. Estimated water damage: negligible (the pitcher was nearly empty, as the filter had not been changed and most personnel had ceased using it). Estimated departmental property loss: $34.99 (retail). No injuries reported. Cause of breakage undetermined.

**WITNESS STATEMENTS:**
- Det. Salazar: "I didn't touch it. Ask Phelan."
- Det. Phelan: "It was already on the edge. Things fall. That's gravity, not a confession."
- Officer Janet Trieu (patrol, first floor): "I heard something break and then I heard laughing, and then the laughing stopped in a way that felt weird, and then someone said 'Just leave it' in a voice I didn't recognize."

**FOLLOW-UP:** None required. Replacement pitcher requisitioned. Form 77-B re-filed.

---

*Cheryl's note, in the margin beside Officer Trieu's statement, in pen that started blue and switched to black mid-sentence as though the first pen died:*

Janet Trieu has good ears. I wish she didn't. There is a version of this report where the Brita pitcher fell because someone's elbow caught it, and two men who have spent fourteen years turning shared annoyance into a kind of communion laughed about it and cleaned it up and moved on. That version is probably true.

But there is also the version where the laughing stopped. Where someone said "Just leave it" in a voice that meant something other than "leave the broken pitcher on the floor." And that version — I don't have documentation for it. I only have Janet Trieu's ears and my own sense, developed over fifteen years of processing paperwork generated by these two men, that by March 7, something had already ended, and only one of them knew it.

I filed the incident summary. I requisitioned the replacement pitcher. These are the things I can do.

The replacement pitcher arrived on March 12. As of this writing, its filter has been changed once, by me, on April 1, because neither of them was going to do it and the water was starting to taste like grief.

That isn't what I meant to type. Like metal. The water tasted like metal.

---

## II.

**ARTIFACT 2-A: TASK FORCE AUTHORIZATION REQUEST, FILED 2:47 PM, MARCH 15**

**REQUESTING OFFICER:** Det. Emmanuel Salazar, Shield #4412
**PROPOSED TASK FORCE DESIGNATION:** Salazar Counterfeiting Working Group (SCWG)
**CASE REFERENCE:** The body of one Terrence Yip, age 41, found March 11 in a dumpster behind a nail salon on Northern Boulevard with two .22-caliber entry wounds and $14,600 in counterfeit fifty-dollar bills distributed among his jacket pockets with what the forensic examiner described as "almost liturgical care" — fifties layered face-up, organized by serial prefix, rubber-banded in stacks of twenty. The bills were high-quality intaglio work. The body fell under Homicide jurisdiction. The bills made it everyone's problem.
**PROPOSED TEAM:**
1. Det. Salazar (lead)
2. Forensic Accountant Linda Chow (Financial Crimes, on loan)
3. Forensic Accountant Marcus Webb (Financial Crimes, on loan — "Linda says she needs a second set of eyes or she 'will spiral'")
4. Officer Darren Smits (patrol, fluent in Cantonese, knows the Northern Blvd. corridor)
5. Retired Det. Arthur Padilla ("has agreed to consult if we cover his MetroCard and he doesn't have to attend any meetings before noon")

---

**ARTIFACT 2-B: TASK FORCE AUTHORIZATION REQUEST, FILED 3:12 PM, MARCH 15**

**REQUESTING OFFICER:** Det. Douglas Phelan, Shield #4471
**PROPOSED TASK FORCE DESIGNATION:** Queens Counterfeiting Initiative (QCI)
**CASE REFERENCE:** Same.
**PROPOSED TEAM:**
1. Det. Phelan (lead)
2. Officer Rosalie Fong (community liaison, Flushing)
3. Retired Det. Idris "Dre" Campbell ("will work for reasons he described as 'none of your business, I'm bored, my wife says I reorganized the garage three times'")
4. A civilian cooperator identified in the file only as "Konstantin" — full name Konstantin Stavridis, operator of a hot dog cart on 37th Street, whose regular route passes within two hundred feet of the gutted mattress warehouse on 48th Avenue where the counterfeiting operation was believed to be centered
5. [A line that was filled in, then scratched out, then written over with the words "TBD — still working on this"]

---

*Cheryl's note, written on a separate sheet and inserted between the two authorization forms:*

Twenty-five minutes. He filed twenty-five minutes after Manny did.

I have been asked, by no one, to comment on the coincidence. So I will comment on it for the record that no one requested.

These two men worked the Astoria drug-lab dismantlement together in 2014. They worked the Jackson Heights double homicide in 2017 — the one with the refrigerator, the one nobody in the precinct can talk about without someone leaving the room. They worked the Corona identity-theft ring in 2019 with the kind of seamless coordination that made the FBI liaison send a note calling their case-building "unusually elegant for NYPD, no offense." Manny builds the paper architecture. Doug walks the streets. Their closure rate for shared cases: 94%. I have the spreadsheet. I built the spreadsheet. No one asked me to build it. I built it because patterns are legible if someone bothers to read them.

They could have collaborated on this case. The jurisdictional overlap made it natural. The case practically *requested* them both. And they forked.

I noticed something else while processing Doug's authorization form. His handwriting has changed. I have fourteen years of Doug Phelan's handwriting passing through my intake window — big, looping letters that took up excess space, letters that implied the form was too small for what he had to say. The Doug Phelan who filed the QCI authorization wrote in letters that were small and careful and stayed inside the boxes. It was the handwriting of someone conserving something. Space, maybe. Or time.

I am noting this for the record. The record does not require it. I am noting it anyway.

---

**ARTIFACT 2-C: GROUP CHAT LOG, "108 HOMICIDE FLOOR 2" (PARTIAL)**

*March 15, 4:18 PM*

**SALAZAR:** Did anyone else file a counterfeiting task force today or just me
**PHELAN:** Define "anyone else"
**SALAZAR:** Doug.
**PHELAN:** Ah
**PHELAN:** Yes
**SALAZAR:** We're on the same floor
**PHELAN:** And yet
**SALAZAR:** You could have walked twelve feet to my desk
**PHELAN:** I could have. But then I would have had to walk twelve feet to your desk, and your desk smells like that protein powder you keep in the drawer that expired in 2022
**TRIEU (patrol):** Is this about the Brita filter again
**SALAZAR:** Janet this is a private conversation
**TRIEU:** It's the floor group chat, Manny
**PHELAN:** It's not about the filter. It's about professional boundaries. Some of us believe in maintaining independent investigative frameworks
**SALAZAR:** "Independent investigative frameworks" is a phrase you have never used before in your life
**PHELAN:** I'm growing
**SALAZAR:** You're being a pain in my ass
**PHELAN:** Also growing

*[Thirteen minutes of no messages]*

**SALAZAR:** You put a civilian hot dog vendor on your task force
**PHELAN:** Konstantin is an asset
**SALAZAR:** He's a hot dog vendor
**PHELAN:** With a CART, Manny. With a PERMANENT CART. Positioned two hundred feet from the target location. He has been conducting inadvertent surveillance for THREE YEARS. The man knows every face, every delivery schedule, every license plate. He is the most accidentally qualified intelligence source in Queens County.
**SALAZAR:** He sells hot dogs
**PHELAN:** He sells hot dogs AND he has eyes, Manny, which is more than I can say for your forensic accountants who have reportedly not left the spreadsheet since Tuesday

---

*Cheryl's note, printed below the chat log:*

I screenshotted this conversation from my own phone because I am in the group chat. Everyone on the second floor is in the group chat. I have never once posted in it. I read every message. I take screenshots when the institutional record requires preservation.

The record does not require preservation of Doug Phelan deploying the word "growing."

I preserved it anyway.

---

**ARTIFACT 2-D: POST-IT NOTE, YELLOW, FOUND ADHERED TO DET. SALAZAR'S MONITOR, DATED MARCH 16 (DATE ESTIMATED PER CHERYL'S INTAKE LOG)**

In Doug Phelan's new, small handwriting:

*"Your filter's overdue. Like your apology for the protein powder smell. — D"*

Below it, in Manny Salazar's all-caps:

*"I'LL CHANGE THE FILTER WHEN YOU CHANGE YOUR ATTITUDE"*

Below that, in Doug's hand again, smaller still:

*"Deal. You first."*

---

*Cheryl's note, in the margin of the photocopy she made of this Post-it before re-pinning it to the monitor:*

This is how they talk. This is how they have always talked. I have 247 Post-it notes in a folder I maintain outside the official filing system. I have never been asked to maintain this folder. I began it in 2012 when I noticed that the Post-it notes left on and around Desks 7 and 8 constituted a more accurate record of the Salazar-Phelan partnership than any case file or performance review.

They do not say things to each other. They leave things for each other to find.

I understand this practice. I relate to it more than I intend to document here.

---

## III.

**ARTIFACT 3-A: EVIDENCE LOG — SALAZAR COUNTERFEITING WORKING GROUP (SCWG), MARCH 18–APRIL 2**

*[Selected entries, annotated by Sgt. Kang-Moretti]*

**March 18, 09:40** — Forensic Accountant Linda Chow submits preliminary financial trace on counterfeit serial prefixes. Seventeen pages, single-spaced. Marcus Webb submits a supplementary appendix that is, upon inspection, a thirty-eight-row Excel printout
narrative_idea_gen_original_prompt:
The Hateful Immortals: A Documentary History of the Greenbriar-Chen Marriage (1847-2024)

In this parallel universe where certain humans develop random superpowers at puberty, historian Dr. Amelia Thornton presents her definitive documentary account of the world's most infamous couple: Margaret Greenbriar, who gained perfect memory, and James Chen, who became unkillable—two people who fell desperately in love in Victorian Boston, got married, and have spent the last 177 years completely unable to divorce because neither can die and Margaret literally cannot forget a single cruel word James has ever said. The documentary traces their reluctant relocations across eras and continents—fleeing each new “special place” (their Parisian apartment, their Buenos Aires vineyard, their Portland bookshop) once neighbors notice they don't age—while Margaret's perfect recall of every argument since 1852 collides with James's infuriating certainty that he'll outlast her grudges. What emerges is a darkly hilarious examination of how immortality transforms the “till death do us part” romance into an endless fish-out-of-water comedy, as two people who genuinely love each other must perpetually adapt to new centuries, new social norms, and the horrible realization that forever is a very long time to be married to someone who still remembers that you called her mother “a pestilent harridan” during the McKinley administration.
